screeningScope: Full-text source, eligibility, taxonomy, and synthesis-readiness review of Rehabilitation & Return to Sport queue positions 19-93. Drafted by Claude Haiku 5.5 and claim-audited against source text by Claude Opus 5.5 (docs/haiku-calibration/).

decisionDefinitions.INCLUDE: Eligible for evidence extraction and synthesis after full-text review.
decisionDefinitions.DEGRADED: A required source or verification element was unavailable.

records.sourceFile: Stress Relaxation and Targeted    Nutrition to Treat Patellar Tendinopathy.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: A case study of one professional male basketball player with MRI-confirmed central core patellar tendinopathy at the inferior pole of the patella. Over about 18 months he did twice-weekly single-leg isometric holds (10 to 30 seconds, above 80% 1RM) plus 15 g gelatin with vitamin C one hour before loading; there was no control group. MRI reactivity fell and an orthopedic surgeon declared the tendon normal at the final scan, the proximal tendon diameter fell from 10.8 mm to 8.2 mm, and the mid-tendon thickened from 5.74 mm to 6.29 mm. Pain decreased, and single-leg isometric strength rose by 156% to 196%, as the author reports.
records.limitations: This is one athlete with no control group, so the gelatin and loading effects cannot be separated. Pain and performance were self-reported or not measured with a formal outcome, and the author states that the injury-rate drop in the team is unquantified.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read this single case as proof that gelatin plus stress-relaxation loading cures patellar tendinopathy in elite athletes, when the paper has no comparison group and reports one player's outcome.

changes: paper.methods: MRI timing wrong ('repeated at 15 and 18 months') -> 15 months after the initial scan and 6 months later, about 12 and 18 months into the program ('15 months after the initial scan) and six months later'); added that baseline MRI used a separate machine

paper.rtp: 'playing more than 25 minutes a game during the program' overstated -> averaged more than 20 minutes per contest, more than 25 minutes only at the final scan ('averaging more than 20 minutes per contest'; 'At the point of the final scan ... playing more than 25 minutes a game')
paper.practicalImplications: causal 'produced' -> 'was followed by' (single uncontrolled case)
paper.limitations: clarified that isometric strength was measured but no on-court performance measure; added scanner change
paper.findings: added body mass change (-2.5 kg) and ~25% proximal diameter decrease
verification.residualConcerns: Single uncontrolled case used to support a rehab protocol; author's team-wide injury reduction claim is anecdotal.

records.sourceFile: Surgically treated pectoralis major tears impact the play and performance of National Football League athletes.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Descriptive epidemiologic case series of NFL players with surgically repaired pectoralis major tears, identified from 80 NFL seasons (1933-2013) using a public transactions archive and confirmed by two investigators. Of 24 players, 20 (83%) returned to play after a mean of 302 days (SD 128); their mean performance score fell from 299.26 before injury to 127.94 after (difference 171.33, P = .033), but the difference was not significant within offensive or defensive players or within draft-round groups.
records.limitations: The sample is small (24 players, 20 with performance data), the tears came from a public archive with little detail on severity, mechanism or surgical technique, and the study has no comparison group. Results are from professional players and may not apply to college or recreational athletes.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could treat the 83% return rate and the 302-day average as a prediction for an individual player, when this is a 24-player case series with no comparison group and no measure of injury severity or surgical technique.

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Case report of one 23-year-old professional footballer with a full-thickness proximal adductor longus avulsion (tendon retracted 3.9 cm on MRI) treated with surgical reattachment five days after injury. He completed an eleven-phase criteria-based return-to-performance pathway, reached 94% of peak speed in grass phase 3, and completed a 45-minute U23 match at 12 weeks, with full regular match play from week 14.
records.limitations: This is a single case with no comparison group and no outcome measures beyond the team's own criteria, so the result describes one course of care rather than an effect of the pathway. Table 1 and Figure 2 values are not fully reproduced in the extracted text, so the numeric criteria could not be checked against the tables.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the 12-week U23 match and 14-week full return as a typical timeline for surgical adductor longus repair, when it is one professional player's course under one club's criteria-based pathway.

changes: paper.findings: said hop measures were within 10% of pre-injury at weeks 6.5 to 7 -> only adductor squeeze and hip ROM were within 10%; SSC/hop needed 80% ('achieving 80% of pre-injury metrics were sufficient'; 'adductor squeeze and hip range of motion were all within 10%')
paper.limitations: said strength thresholds came from earlier studies by the same group -> thresholds cite Mosler et al. 2017 and Serner et al. 2020, other groups
verification.residualConcerns: Year 2024 rests on the online-first date (20 Sep 2024); no volume or issue is printed.

records.sourceFile: Testing Limb Symmetry and Asymmetry After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury - 4 Considerations to Increase Its Utility.pdf
records.degradedReason: The article's own DOI is not printed in the extracted text. The journal header shows Volume 46, Number 4, August 2024 and pages from 406, but no DOI appears, and reference-list DOIs were not used.

changes: paper.citation: page range incomplete ('406') -> 406-414 (running footers print pages 406 through 414 with 'VOLUME 46 | NUMBER 4 | AUGUST 2024')
verification.residualConcerns: DOI not printed anywhere in the text; operator should verify externally before upgrading. Paper bears on return-to-sport testing after ACL reconstruction.

records.sourceFile: The British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification grading system as a predictor of return to play following hamstrings injury in professional soccer players.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Retrospective cohort of 39 primary hamstring strain injuries in 30 adult male professional players at one English club over 2010 to 2019, where each injury had an MRI within 7 days of onset. Two musculoskeletal radiologists graded the MRIs with the British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC) and with Peetron's system, and the grades were compared with return to play (mean 16.5 days). BAMIC grade correlated weakly with return to play (r = 0.32, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.58, p = 0.05), oedema length correlated weakly and not significantly (r = 0.3, p = 0.06), cross-sectional area did not correlate (r = 0.02), and the two grading systems agreed only slightly (kappa = 0.21).
records.limitations: The sample is 39 injuries from one club, so the confidence intervals are wide and the model explained only 16% of the variance in return to play. The design is retrospective, and the two classifications disagree enough that the grade cannot be read as a precise prediction for an individual player.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read BAMIC as a reliable predictor of an individual player's return date, when the paper reports a weak correlation from a small single-club sample.

changes: evidenceSummary: added that the 39 injuries came from 30 players and the mean return to play ('39 HSI from 30 professional football players'; 'overall mean for RTP was 16.5 (SD 12.2 ...) days')
verification.residualConcerns: Return-to-play topic. Text is the journal pre-proof; year 2022 taken from the 'Please cite' line, and no volume or pages are printed. Several players contributed more than one injury, which the correlations do not account for.

records.sourceFile: The Impact of Daylight Exposure on Injured Athletes - Implications for Rehabilitation.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Narrative review of daylight and sunlight in athletes' injury rehabilitation, using PubMed, PsycINFO and Google Scholar (1960 to October 2023, German or English) with no design or quality criteria. The authors found no study of daylight exposure on the prevalence or rehabilitation of sports injuries. They organise related evidence on vitamin D, cognitive-behavioural processes, circadian timing and visual light processing, mostly from non-injured or non-athlete samples, small studies and animal models.
records.limitations: The search was not systematic and applied no study quality criteria, and the review itself calls its answer exploratory. Almost none of the cited evidence comes from injured athletes, and the intervention in the paper is the authors' own proposal, not something that has been tested.
records.synthesisCaution: Reading the proposed daylight or dawn-simulation routine, and the sleep, hormone and pain findings from healthy or non-athlete samples, as proven aids that speed injury rehabilitation or return to play.

changes: paper.findings: Fowler et al sample given as 'ten male athletes' -> two groups of ten male athletes, circadian-timed light vs no intervention ('two groups of ten male athletes, one group receiving light exposure adapted to the individual circadian rhythm, and the other with no intervention')

paper.limitations: 'the sleep studies cited range from one to 20 participants' -> the daylight and sleep studies in clinical populations (Parkinson's, glaucoma, Alzheimer's, musculoskeletal disease) had one to 20 participants ('small participant numbers ranging from one to 20')

paper.limitations: 'Table 1 effects come from healthy or non-injured samples' (sample health not stated) -> from studies that were not of injured athletes in rehabilitation ('there are no existing studies on the impact of daylight on the psychological and sleep parameters of athletes in rehabilitation')
paper.athleteDev: 'vitamin D findings in athletes are mixed' -> findings differed between athletes (Michalczyk) and non-athletes (Carswell); 'small studies' -> one small study (Fowler et al.)
paper.findings: Carswell exposure given as 'sunlight' -> artificial sunlight ('through both artificial sunlight exposure and vitamin D supplementation')
